questions.explanation: Very few candidates recognised that a percentage increase in one force needs the same percentage increase in the other two. With the directions unchanged, the three forces must still close into the same triangle, just scaled up, so Q and R rise by 10% as well: A. In this diagram Q = P and R = P√2, so everything scales together. B and D were popular, which shows candidates thinking Q and R rise by different proportions. Many chose C: they took Q up by 10%, then worked out the absolute rise in R and treated it as a percentage. With P = Q = 100 N, R goes from 141 N to 156 N, a rise of 14 N = 10√2 N, which is the figure in C. Compare ratios, not raw increases.

Many candidates correctly saw that a solid steel object of the same dimensions has greater mass and so greater weight, while the upthrust stays the same, so it needs a greater speed before the resistive forces balance the weight: A. The most popular wrong answer was B. The hollow object already reached its terminal velocity before it hit the ground, so dropping it from higher up changes nothing. Candidates who pictured an object falling without air resistance, where more height does mean more speed, or who had not noticed the object reached terminal velocity, chose it. A different starting speed does not change the terminal velocity either, only how soon it is reached.

The ball is decelerating, so the resultant force on it is upwards and equal to ma = 4.50 × 800 = 3600 N. That is the resultant force, though, and the question asks for the force from the sand. The sand's force must also hold up the weight: F − mg = ma, so F = 4.50 × 800 + 4.50 × 9.81 = 3600 + 44 = 3644 N, which rounds to 3640 N, D. The vast majority of candidates stopped at 3600 N (C) and never added the weight. A small number gave the weight, 44.1 N (A), perhaps picturing an equilibrium. Draw both forces on the ball before you write the equation.

The question asks which statement is not a requirement. Forces in a third-law pair are equal in magnitude, opposite in direction and act on different objects, but the objects need not touch: gravity and magnetism act at a distance. So C is not a requirement. B was the most popular wrong answer, which shows the common misconception that the two forces of a third-law pair act on the same object. That belongs to equilibrium, where the forces on one object balance. Candidates often confuse the two.

The hydrometer floats, so its weight equals the upthrust, which is ρgV for the volume V of liquid displaced. The weight does not change, so a less dense liquid needs a greater displaced volume. The hydrometer sits lower, and the length h above the liquid decreases: B. Many candidates chose D, perhaps confusing what h measures: it is the part of the tube above the liquid, so a denser liquid, which pushes the hydrometer up, makes h larger. Mark on the diagram what h actually measures before you decide which way it moves.

Both conditions are needed for equilibrium: no resultant force and no resultant torque. B states one of them as a requirement and is correct. Very few chose A, so that misconception is rare. Many chose C and D, each of which treats one condition as enough: a couple has no resultant force but still turns the object, so D fails, and an object with no moments but a resultant force would accelerate, so C fails. Few chose B, which suggests the idea of a resultant torque was unfamiliar.

Many candidates used the energy stored to find the extension: E = ½kx2, so x = √(2 × 0.010 / 22.5) = 0.030 m = 30 mm. The question asks for the unstretched length and 80 mm is the stretched length, so the answer is 80 − 30 = 50 mm, B. Many stopped at the extension, 30 mm (A). C was the most popular wrong answer: leaving out the ½ gives an extension of about 21 mm and a length of about 60 mm. D adds the extension to the stretched length, which means the original and final lengths were swapped. Re-read the last line of the question before choosing.

All the options were chosen frequently and fairly equally, so the diffraction grating equation was not being applied with confidence. The grating spacing d and the angle are the same for both wavelengths, so nλ = d sinθ gives n<sub>X</sub>λ<sub>X</sub> = n<sub>Y</sub>λ<sub>Y</sub>, and with n<sub>X</sub> = 2, λ<sub>X</sub>/λ<sub>Y</sub> = n<sub>Y</sub>/2. The order n<sub>Y</sub> has to be a whole number, so the ratio can be 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0 and so on. Of the options only 1.50 fits, with n<sub>Y</sub> = 3: D. The other three would need an order of 0.5, 1.5 or 2.5.

Most candidates chose A or B, so they can tell nodes from antinodes. The graph asks for the amplitude, though, not the displacement. Amplitude is never negative, it is zero at each node and largest at each antinode. The closed end of the tube is a node, so the graph starts at zero and its humps meet the axis at the nodes: A. B and D were chosen by those who drew a displacement graph, which passes below the axis. That mixes up displacement, a vector, with amplitude.

Most candidates correctly selected C, so the definition of potential difference was well understood. The energy transferred is W = QV: the charge that passed times the p.d. The time is unknown, so anything that needs the time is out. A was the most popular wrong answer: I and V give the power, VI, and you would then need the time to get an energy. Candidates mixed up power and energy.

Many candidates correctly selected B. The block holds nV charge carriers, each of charge q, and each takes an average time t to pass through, so the charge passing per second is I = nVq / t. C was the most popular wrong answer: candidates realised the equation needs the time in the denominator but used the wrong quantity on top. D was also popular, perhaps from confusing the volume V with the drift speed v in I = Anvq. Check what each letter stands for before you substitute.

Many candidates correctly recalled that the resistance of a filament lamp varies with the current in it: a larger current heats the filament, the metal ions vibrate more, and the resistance increases: A. The other three go the other way. The resistance of an LDR falls as the light intensity increases, the resistance of a diode falls when the current through it increases, and a thermistor's resistance falls as its temperature rises. The wrong answers were chosen evenly, with no single one standing out.

Few candidates used R = ρL/A together with the constant volume. Halving the diameter makes the area a quarter of the original. The volume is unchanged, so the length becomes four times as long. R is proportional to L / A, so it goes up by 4 × 4 = 16: D. C, 4R, was the most popular choice: those candidates correctly found that the area drops by a factor of 4, but did not allow for the longer wire. Whenever a wire is stretched or reformed with constant volume, change length and area together.

Few candidates chose B. There are several routes. The first reading, 12 V across 4.0 Ω, means 3.0 A, so the internal resistance of 2.0 Ω has 6.0 V across it and the e.m.f. is 18 V. With a second 4.0 Ω resistor in parallel the external resistance is 2.0 Ω, equal to the internal resistance, so each takes half the e.m.f.: the voltmeter reads 9.0 V. All three wrong answers were selected frequently, with C marginally the most, which suggests candidates thought the added resistor had no effect on the terminal p.d. It does, because the current rises and more of the e.m.f. is lost across the internal resistance. Learn the effect of internal resistance on terminal p.d.
